question.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}-{y}^{4})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{4}-{y}^{4})\,j \\  & =4{x}^{3}\,i-4{y}^{3}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =4{cos}^{3}⁡t\,i-4{sin}^{3}⁡t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(4{cos}^{3}⁡t\,i-4{sin}^{3}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t-4{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$
